name: Bebop
workload: BenchmarkDotNet serialize/deserialize latency of tiny/simple/complex POCOs (once and in bulk), comparing Bebop (Message and Struct variants) against Newtonsoft.Json, System.Text.Json, Google.Protobuf, and MessagePack-CSharp, in an independent third-party benchmark repo.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize complex POCO once: BebopStruct 166.1 ns vs Protobuf 1,051.4 ns (~6.3x faster) and vs MessagePack 1,584.6 ns (~9.5x faster); BebopMessage 231.7 ns similarly ~4.5x faster than Protobuf. Repo README states Bebop is 'the fastest in every benchmark, serialization and deserialization' among the tested formats, and Protobuf becomes 'the slowest of the binary serializers' on deserialization.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, 1 CPU, 32 logical / 16 physical cores, Windows 10
tradeoffs: Bebop also targets TypeScript, Rust, Dart, C, and other languages via its own IDL/codegen, but the cited numeric evidence here is specifically for its C# implementation. Requires a `.bop` schema and code generation step (like Protobuf), unlike schema-less formats.
caveats: The independent benchmark repo (ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks) is small (6 stars) and was last updated in 2021, so it predates recent Bebop/Protobuf/.NET releases; results may not reflect current versions. It is however a genuinely third-party, non-Bebop-affiliated benchmark with full BenchmarkDotNet environment info published, and Bebop's own docs/HN discussion corroborate a large speed advantage over Protobuf.
found_via: WebSearch: query='Bebop serialization benchmark faster than protobuf flatbuffers github' -> github.com/ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks

name: qdf (Quick Data Format)
workload: Wire size and allocations for batches of realistic structured records (OTLP traces, logs, RTB bids, events, IoT float series) encoded record-for-record by json/msgpack/protobuf/flatbuffers/qdf on the same fixtures, via a reproducible `scripts/compare.sh` benchmark suite.
claimed_speedup: qdf smaller than Protobuf on every one of 5 batch fixtures at the compression tier: RTB -38%, IoT -29%, OTLP -68%, Logs -60%, Events -39% (up to 68% smaller than Protobuf per README). On a 5,000-row Active-Directory export, qdf OptBalanced is 2.1x smaller and 2.1x faster to encode and ~7x faster to decode than encoding/json, ~1.8x smaller/~2x faster to decode than msgpack. Author honestly notes FlatBuffers still wins raw encode-allocation and single-tiny-message size, and Protobuf/FlatBuffers win raw decode throughput.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26, default build, benchmark suite in bench/ module run with `-count=6`
tradeoffs: Go-only, pure-Go, no schema/IDL (struct-tag based, alpha format that 'still moves'). Wins are on batches with cross-record repetition; single tiny messages favor Protobuf/FlatBuffers per author's own comparison. Compression tier trades encode CPU for size (e.g. ~70 MB/s vs ~1100 MB/s for the balanced tier on float data).
caveats: Small project (26 stars), alpha status, format not yet frozen. Benchmark hardware is a single named laptop CPU rather than a controlled server; author explicitly flags this ('speed numbers are machine-specific').
found_via: gh search repos topic:binary-serialization --sort stars -> alex60217101990/qdf

name: Quarry
workload: Encode/decode ops-per-second and bytes-per-record for telemetry and large-payload workloads, comparing Quarry's C and C++ generated code (BRF wire format) against protoc-generated Protobuf C++ (default and Arena) code, five aggregated CI runs.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, honestly reported: Protobuf wins telemetry encode/decode (18.81M/13.48M ops/s vs Quarry C 9.69M/5.45M) and large encode (1.60M vs 0.48M), but Quarry C wins large-payload decode (0.85M ops/s vs Protobuf C++ 0.57M and Protobuf Arena 0.45M, ~1.5-1.9x faster). Quarry's BRF format is larger on the wire than Protobuf in the tested cases (e.g. 60 vs 16 bytes/record for telemetry).
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763, Linux/x86_64 GitHub-hosted CI runner
tradeoffs: Header-only/deterministic-footprint native runtime (claimed zero native runtime size) vs Protobuf's external runtime library. Larger wire format than Protobuf on tested workloads. Very new/low-adoption project; README explicitly warns shared-runner timing is 'informational' and depends on hardware/compiler/optimization/runtime/workload.
caveats: Extremely low star count (4) and single-maintainer project; only a narrow win (large-payload decode) rather than an across-the-board win — reported honestly per instructions rather than cherry-picked. GitHub Actions shared runners add benchmark noise, acknowledged by the author.
found_via: gh search repos "binary serialization" language:C++ --sort stars -> ip332/quarry

name: rkyv
baseline: Cap'n Proto, FlatBuffers, Protocol Buffers (via prost/protobuf crates), MessagePack (via rmp-serde/msgpacker/zerompk)
workload: Serialize/deserialize/zero-copy-access speed and size on structured Rust datasets (HTTP log records, 3D mesh data, Minecraft save data) via Criterion benchmarks in the independently-hosted rust_serialization_benchmark suite.
claimed_speedup: On the 'log' dataset: rkyv serialize 178.87 µs vs FlatBuffers 763.63 µs (~4.3x faster) and vs Cap'n Proto 480.15 µs (~2.7x faster); rkyv unvalidated zero-copy access ~1.09 ns and unvalidated deserialize 8.33 µs vs FlatBuffers unvalidated access 2.18 ns / deserialize 42.2 µs. Results are workload-dependent: on 'minecraft_savedata' and other datasets rkyv trails the fastest library (e.g. ~38-54% of best relative serialize speed).
hardware: AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, 4 vCPUs (Hyper-V virtualized), x86_64
tradeoffs: Rust-only, no official C API, so not directly usable from C++ (qualifies under the 'non-C++ implementations welcome' rule). Zero-copy access model requires careful handling of untrusted input (validation feature adds cost, shown separately in the 'validated upfront with error' benchmark rows). Not a schema/IDL system like Cap'n Proto/FlatBuffers/Protobuf — Rust-type-driven instead.
caveats: Benchmark repo (rust_serialization_benchmark) is maintained by rkyv's own author plus collaborators, not a fully independent third party, though it is public, reproducible, and covers dozens of competing libraries fairly. Original rkyv-authored blog post 'rkyv is faster than...' is now a dead/redirected domain, so this entry relies on the maintained benchmark repo instead. Relative performance varies significantly by dataset/workload.
found_via: HN Algolia: query=faster%20than%20flatbuffers -> 'Rkyv is faster than {bincode, capnp, cbor, flatbuffers, postcard, prost}' -> github.com/rkyv/rkyv -> github.com/djkoloski/rust_serialization_benchmark

name: YaFF (Yet another Flat Format)
workload: Median time to read every field out of an already-serialized buffer, for flat messages (10/100 uint64 fields) and a 3-level hierarchical message under hot (~2KB working set) and cold (~512MB working set) access patterns, using google/benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Flat Layout reads are ~25-50x faster than Protobuf and ~2-2.5x faster than FlatBuffers on flat messages (e.g. 100-field flat read: 25.99ns YaFF vs 1383.74ns Protobuf vs 54.81ns FlatBuffers); hierarchical hot access is ~25x faster than Protobuf and ~3.5x faster than FlatBuffers
compiler_and_flags: Clang 20.1.8, Release build, benchmarks built with google/benchmark
tradeoffs: Still requires an existing .proto schema (built as a companion physical layout for Protobuf, not a schema replacement); adds adaptive-layout complexity; C++ only today, multi-language bindings are roadmap items
caveats: Very young project under active development; benchmark is first-party but methodology, exact hardware, and compiler are fully disclosed (meets the Tier A bar); authors note absolute numbers depend on the EPYC 7713's DDR4 memory subsystem, though they claim the relative ratios generalize.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic serialization --language c++ --sort stars
GitHub: gh search repos topic:flatbuffers --sort stars, then opened yandex/yaff README and docs/benchmarks

name: greenpack
workload: Marshal/Unmarshal microbenchmarks of a fixed struct (name, birthday, phone, siblings, spouse, money) across ~20 Go serialization libraries, using Go's testing/benchmark tool, in the companion go_serialization_benchmarks shootout repo.
claimed_speedup: README states greenpack reads are 6% faster and writes 15% faster than Gogoprotobuf-based Protocol Buffers, with zero allocation on write (Gogoprotobuf allocates). Raw shootout numbers: GreenPackMarshal 129 ns/op (0 B/op) vs GogoprotobufMarshal 152 ns/op (64 B/op) and vs ProtobufMarshal 936 ns/op (200 B/op).
tradeoffs: Pure Go, code-generation based (like msgp/msgpack), msgpack2-compatible wire format for cross-language interoperability. Modest win margin (6-15%) over Protobuf, not a dramatic speedup; author explicitly notes ZebraPack and CapNProto/Gencode can be faster in some cases.
caveats: The specific comparison numbers come from the go_serialization_benchmarks suite, last updated 2017 with a beta-era Go compiler (1.8beta2) on old hardware — results are dated and margins this small could shift with modern Go/Protobuf versions. greenpack itself remains actively maintained (2026 commits).
found_via: gh search repos "faster than protobuf" --sort stars -> glycerine/greenpack

name: JSON BinPack
baseline: Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, MessagePack (and Apache Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile, FlexBuffers)
workload: Encoded size of 400+ real-world JSON documents (SchemaStore test suite, 36-category taxonomy) compared across 12+ binary serialization formats, schema-driven and schema-less.
claimed_speedup: JSON BinPack is as space-efficient or more space-efficient than every one of 12+ alternative formats tested in every considered case; e.g. ESLint config sample: 64 bytes vs 1,141 bytes JSON (~94% reduction); also typically beats GZIP/LZMA/LZ4 at max compression for small/medium documents.
tradeoffs: Dual-licensed (AGPL-3.0-or-later or paid commercial license) — AGPL's network-copyleft is a real adoption barrier for closed-source SaaS use. Space-efficiency focused, not runtime-efficiency focused; project's own FAQ recommends FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto instead when zero-copy runtime speed matters. Requires JSON Schema 2020-12 definitions for schema-driven mode.
caveats: Compiler flags and hardware/CPU model for the benchmark run are not published, so it falls short of Tier A despite being methodologically rigorous (peer-examined MSc dissertation at Oxford, CAR Hoare prize, arXiv preprints 2201.02089/2201.03051/2211.12799, public benchmark code and raw results). Benchmark measures encoded byte size, not wall-clock throughput/latency, against protobuf/capnp/flatbuffers/msgpack reference implementations.
found_via: arXiv: search_query=abs:%22FlatBuffers%22+OR+abs:%22Cap%27n+Proto%22 -> arXiv:2211.12799 'Benchmarking JSON BinPack' -> github.com/sourcemeta/jsonbinpack

name: Karmem
workload: Go benchmark (testing/benchmark) encode/decode of an object-API generated struct, both native (Go) and inside WebAssembly (Wazero runtime), on Apple M1 hardware.
claimed_speedup: Karmem ~10x faster than FlatBuffers: native EncodeObjectAPI 0.51ms vs 2.54ms (-79.85%), DecodeObjectAPI 0.20ms vs 3.57ms (-94.30%); inside WASM/Wazero EncodeObjectAPI 4.0ms vs 17.2ms (-76.51%), DecodeObjectAPI 1.9ms vs 50.7ms (-96.18%). Also zero allocations vs FlatBuffers' allocations per op.
compiler_and_flags: Go compiler (version unstated), go test -bench with benchstat comparison
tradeoffs: Designed primarily for WebAssembly host/guest data sharing (TinyGo/WASM), not general-purpose RPC; author states FlatBuffers 'causes panics due to lack of bound-checking' motivating the project. No Rust/C++ note beyond Go/TinyGo/AssemblyScript targets claimed in docs.
caveats: Repo has had no commits since March 2023 (>3 years), so it is abandoned despite the strong numbers; Go compiler version and optimization flags are not stated in the benchmark output, capping this below Tier A.
found_via: HN Algolia: query=faster%20than%20flatbuffers -> 'Karmem: A fast binary serialization format faster than Google Flatbuffers' -> github.com/inkeliz/karmem

name: Simple Binary Encoding (SBE)
workload: Serialize/deserialize a small trading domain object (Account + Wallet + 3 Orders, ~120-280 bytes on the wire) via chronoxor's CppBenchmark-based CppSerialization suite, comparing Cap'n Proto, FastBinaryEncoding, FlatBuffers, Protobuf, SBE, zpp::bits, and JSON.
claimed_speedup: ~9.2x faster serialize (35ns vs 322ns) and ~6.75x faster deserialize (52ns vs 351ns) than Protobuf
compiler_and_flags: CppBenchmark harness, "Process configuration: release"; exact compiler name/version used for the published table is not stated (repo's own CI covers GCC, Clang and MSVC)
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 10 cores (10 physical), 2.4GHz, macOS 24.5.0 (one of several per-run hardware configs logged in the repo)
tradeoffs: Requires an SBE XML schema and code generator; designed around FIX-derived low-latency financial messaging, less flexible than Protobuf for evolving/optional fields
caveats: Benchmark run by a third party (chronoxor, unaffiliated with SBE's aeron-io maintainers) rather than SBE's own team, which makes this a reasonably independent Tier-B source; the message under test is tiny and fixed-size, so results may not generalize to larger/variable-length messages.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:flatbuffers --sort stars surfaced chronoxor/CppSerialization, which benchmarks SBE against Protobuf

name: ZebraPack
workload: Same go_serialization_benchmarks shootout: Marshal/Unmarshal microbenchmarks of a fixed struct across ~20 Go serialization libraries using Go's testing/benchmark tool.
claimed_speedup: Fastest marshal (write) of all tested libraries in the shootout: ZebraPackMarshal 120 ns/op (0 B/op) vs GoprotobufMarshal 500 ns/op (~4.2x faster), ProtobufMarshal 936 ns/op (~7.8x faster), CapNProtoMarshal 498 ns/op (~4.2x faster), and FlatBufferMarshal 379 ns/op (~3.2x faster). Also 0 B/op allocation on marshal.
tradeoffs: Author's own README says use greenpack instead now ('a more recent alternative'). Go-only, code-generation based like msgp, msgpack2-compatible wire format for other-language interop.
caveats: Harvested as the top marshal-speed winner from the go_serialization_benchmarks shootout per 'harvest the winners' instruction. Explicitly superseded by greenpack and unmaintained since 2018 (>3 years, abandoned); benchmark data is from 2017 on an old Go beta compiler, so absolute numbers are stale even though the repo/data are public and reproducible.

name: Apache Fory (C++)
workload: Serialize/deserialize three C++ structs of increasing complexity (NumericStruct, Sample, MediaContent) using Google Benchmark, comparing Fory's C++ implementation against Protobuf.
claimed_speedup: 1.2x-4.5x higher throughput than Protobuf across cases: MediaContent serialize 4.5x (2,254,915 vs 504,410 ops/sec), MediaContent deserialize 1.9x, Sample serialize/deserialize ~1.3x, NumericStruct serialize 1.6x / deserialize 1.2x
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build, C++17 (repo states GCC 8+/Clang 7+/MSVC 2019+ are supported); exact compiler/version used for the published numbers is not stated
hardware: Darwin 24.5.0, arm64, 12 physical/12 logical cores, 48GB RAM (specific CPU model, e.g. which Apple silicon chip, not named)
tradeoffs: Much larger, multi-language xlang framework rather than a lightweight C++-only library; C++ support is newer and less battle-tested than Fory's Java implementation
caveats: First-party benchmark (Apache Fory's own repo); exact CPU model and compiler version not disclosed; C++ gains (1.2-4.5x) are more modest than several other zero-copy competitors in this list, unlike Fory's much larger claimed Java-only wins (up to 170x vs JDK serialization, a different comparison not against Protobuf).

name: fernBuffer
workload: Encoded byte size of 10 representative JSON-like payloads (logs, flat records, hex strings, sparse nulls, repeated strings, float/int/bool arrays, tiny objects, deep nesting) encoded by fernBuffer vs Python's msgpack library.
claimed_speedup: Smaller than MessagePack on 7 of 10 test cases, e.g. log entries 10.9 KB vs 15.1 KB (~28% smaller), sparse nulls 903 B vs 1.9 KB (~52% smaller), repeated strings 557 B vs 1.2 KB (~54% smaller); but larger than MessagePack on float array, int array, bool array, and tiny objects cases.
tradeoffs: Author explicitly labels it 'more of a prototype / proof of concept ... bugs or flaws may exist'. C library with a small C API (usable from C++), also exposes a ctypes-based Python binding. No zero-copy/schema features.
caveats: No compiler/hardware stated for the size-only benchmark; results are honestly mixed (worse than MessagePack on 3-4 of 10 cases, per the project's own table). Tiny, single-author, very new project.
found_via: gh search repos "binary serialization" language:C++ --sort stars -> Escartem/fernBuffer

name: HyperSerializer
workload: BenchmarkDotNet serialize+deserialize of 1,000,000 instances of a 10-field 'Test' class (Guid, int, long, DateTime, uint, decimal, TimeSpan, enum, string), comparing HyperSerializer, MessagePack, Protobuf, and ApexSerializer.
claimed_speedup: README states HyperSerializer is 'up to 16x faster than MessagePack and Protobuf, and 2x faster than MemoryPack' with roughly equivalent or better memory allocation; elsewhere states 'roughly 3x faster than ApexSerializer and 18x faster than MessagePack and Protobuf'.
tradeoffs: Contract-less: relies on identical field/property layout between source and destination types, no versioning/schema-evolution support; mismatched types can throw or silently misdecode. .NET only, span-based, described by its author as a 'champion/challenger (C++ vs C#) experiment'.
caveats: Benchmark numbers are presented only as PNG charts in the README (Time.png / Space.png), not as a text table, and no CPU model or BenchmarkDotNet environment block is published in visible README text, so this is capped at Tier C despite using BenchmarkDotNet internally. The two stated ratios (16x vs 18x) are also inconsistent between sections of the same README.
found_via: HN Algolia: query=faster%20than%20protobuf -> gh search repos "faster than protobuf" --sort stars -> adam-dot-cohen/HyperSerializer

name: MTS-1 (Lightweight Delta-Encoded Telemetry Format)
workload: Synthetic telemetry payload size comparison (storage footprint) of MTS-1 against JSON, JSON Lines, CBOR, MessagePack, and Protocol Buffers for low-resource/offline-first system health monitoring.
claimed_speedup: Reported ~5.4% smaller than MessagePack and 74.6-74.7% smaller than JSON on the paper's synthetic S1 dataset (MTS-1 1.39 MB vs MessagePack 1.47 MB). Protocol Buffers was explicitly excluded from quantitative testing by the authors ('schema compilation requirements incompatible with dynamic monitoring scenarios').
tradeoffs: No throughput/latency numbers at all, only payload size; Protobuf, one of the category's core baselines, was deliberately not benchmarked. No implementation language, code repository, or reference implementation could be found.
caveats: No code repository found for MTS-1; this is a January 2026 arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed), single-author, with only synthetic benchmarking and no production validation, and a fairly modest (5.4%) win over MessagePack. Included as a paper-only research-section entry per instructions since it directly compares against a baseline in the target list.
found_via: arXiv: search_query=abs:%22Protocol+Buffers%22+AND+abs:%22performance%22 -> arXiv:2601.01602 'MTS-1: A Lightweight Delta-Encoded Telemetry Format...'

name: ProtoCache
workload: Decode+traverse+deallocate (and reflection-based decode+traverse) of a Protobuf-schema message, plus full serialization of the complex twitter.proto dataset, comparing Protobuf, ProtoCache, ProtoCacheEX, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, and Fory.
claimed_speedup: ~20x faster decode+traverse+dealloc than Protobuf (132ns vs 2620ns); ~30x faster with reflection (270ns vs 8189ns); ProtoCacheEX serializes twitter.proto ~2.1x faster than Protobuf (101us vs 215us)
benchmark_url: https://github.com/PeterRK/protocache (README.md benchmark tables; code in test/benchmark)
tradeoffs: Requires an existing Protobuf schema/toolchain (protoc + protoc-gen-pccx plugin); ProtoCache's own plain Serialize is actually slower than Protobuf per its own table (6493ns vs 557ns) — the win is specifically on decode/traverse, not on encode
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, or compiler flags disclosed for the timing benchmark, only that it is a Release-ish native-optimized build; small project (83 stars); numbers are first-party.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:flatbuffers --sort stars, then opened PeterRK/protocache README

name: zzzJSON
workload: Parse+stringify wall time (ms) over nativejson-benchmark-style corpora (no-number JSON, JSON from Taobao, all-JSON-combined, random short/long JSON), run via the repo's build.sh
claimed_speedup: 'All JSON Above' total time 166ms (zzzjson) vs 220ms (RapidJSON) (~1.33x); Random Short JSON 38ms vs 56ms (~1.47x); Random Long JSON 29ms vs 45ms (~1.55x); No-Number JSON 149ms vs 224ms (~1.50x) (derived from page data)

tradeoffs: Pure C, single header, 'parse on use' lazy number handling; no SIMD, so it does not compete with simdjson/yyjson-class parsers, only with DOM libraries like RapidJSON/nlohmann/cJSON
caveats: Numbers are from 2018-era hardware and an old compiler (GCC 7.3); repository has had no commits since 2020-12-26; LICENSE file is an informal public-domain-style dedication ('do whatever you want with it'), not a recognized SPDX id, and grants no patent rights

name: easyjson
workload: Marshal/unmarshal of a 13KB Twitter-search-style JSON document (9KB minified), an 80-byte small-request case, and a ~500KB large-request case (50 concatenated samples), using easyjson's codegen'd marshalers
claimed_speedup: 'easyjson is roughly 5-6 times faster than the standard encoding/json for unmarshaling, and 3-4 times faster for non-concurrent marshaling. Concurrent marshaling is 6-7x faster if marshaling to a writer' (verbatim from README)
tradeoffs: Requires an ahead-of-time codegen step (easyjson -all file.go), so it is not a drop-in import swap like go-json/sonic; default fast path uses unsafe
caveats: No CPU model, Go version, or compiler flags stated anywhere in the README; the speedups are given as rounded 'roughly N-Mx' ranges rather than exact benchmark output

name: Cista++
workload: Serialize/deserialize/traverse a graph of nodes and edges (object-oriented graph with pointers/indices) using the 'offset' and 'raw' variants of Cista++, compared to cereal, Cap'n Proto, and FlatBuffers
claimed_speedup: Cista++ 'offset': serialize 4ms vs cereal 216ms (~54x), deserialize 0.16ms vs cereal 111ms (~694x), deserialize+traverse 66ms vs cereal 174ms (~2.6x); compile time (clang-7) 1.351s vs cereal 1.827s
tradeoffs: The zero-copy 'offset' variant requires reading/writing in a fixed pointer-offset layout (no relocation), so both ends must share pointer width/endianness; the 'raw' variant (native pointers, relocatable) is far slower to serialize (3555ms) because of the extra relocation pass. Not schema-evolution-friendly like protobuf/capnproto without opt-in versioning.
caveats: Benchmark numbers come from felixguendling's own companion repo (cpp-serialization-benchmark), so it is first-party, but methodology (code, compiler, OS, exact CPU) is fully public, which is why it still qualifies for tier A. The main cista README shows a second run of the same benchmark with different absolute numbers (72ms vs 239ms serialize) from a different session; both point the same direction. The very large deserialize speedup vs cereal is an architectural effect of zero-copy access (no parsing step), not a benchmarking artifact.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic serialization --language c++ --sort stars
GitHub: gh search repos topic:serialization language:C++ --sort stars, then opened felixguendling/cista README and its linked benchmark repo

name: struct_pack (yalantinglibs)
workload: Serialize/deserialize three struct shapes (a 4-field 'rect', a 4-field 'person', and a nested 'Monster'-style struct) for one million iterations each, compared to protobuf, msgpack, and flatbuffers, using compile-time reflection (no macros for aggregate types)
claimed_speedup: (derived from page data, read off the serialize-speed chart) struct_pack ~15-20ns vs protobuf ~320ns for 'rect' (~16-20x), ~120ns vs ~530ns for 'person' (~4.4x), ~650ns vs ~2900ns for 'monster' (~4.5x); also far ahead of msgpack (~1100-8000ns) on the same cases
tradeoffs: Works best on aggregate structs; non-aggregate types (private members, custom order) need the YLT_REFL macro. Forward/backward compatibility requires explicitly wrapping new fields in struct_pack::compatible<T,version>. Ships as part of a large multi-library monorepo (yalantinglibs) rather than a standalone single-purpose dependency.
caveats: Numbers were read visually off bar charts (PNG images) in the docs rather than a text table, so the figures above are estimates from the chart axes, not exact values; confidence is lowered accordingly. The docs compare against protobuf/msgpack/flatbuffers, not Boost.Serialization or cereal directly, hence baseline_in_list=false.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "struct_pack"

claimed_speedup: thekvs suite: yas 302.7ms total vs boost 1195.04ms (~3.9x) and cereal 1052.46ms (~3.5x); fraillt suite (GCC 11): yas 2286ms ser/1770ms des vs boost 15126ms/12724ms (~6.6x/~7.2x) and cereal 10777ms/9088ms (~4.7x/~5.1x)

name: bitsery
workload: Serialize/deserialize a nested 'Monster' struct (vectors, strings, enums, weapons) for 300,000 samples, compiled with GCC 11 and Clang 12.0.1 on Ubuntu 20.04 x64 (fraillt/cpp_serializers_benchmark suite)
claimed_speedup: bitsery 1119-1524ms ser / 1166-1561ms des vs boost 15126-16011ms ser / 12724-13017ms des (~10-14x faster), and vs cereal 9977-10777ms ser / 8565-9088ms des (~7-9x faster)

name: Parshred
workload: Single-threaded DOM parse of XML files from 64KB to 128MB (bench/bench_dom, median of repeated runs), measuring MB/s and comparing against RapidXml and pugixml on the same reference machine
claimed_speedup: vs pugixml: 2572 vs 1465 MB/s (~1.76x) at 64KB; 2722 vs 821 MB/s (~3.3x) at 1MB; 2519 vs 1585 MB/s (~1.59x) at 16MB; 1678 vs 641 MB/s (~2.6x) at 64MB; 1317 vs 712 MB/s (~1.85x) at 128MB (derived from page data); vs RapidXml: within ~5% at 64KB-16MB, 1.5x-1.83x faster at 64MB+ (up to 2.4x observed on other machines per the README)

name: simdxml
workload: End-to-end XPath query benchmarks (sxq CLI vs pugixml vs xmllint) on real-world corpora - DBLP 5.1GB //article, PubMed 195MB //MeshHeading, 10MB attribute-heavy //record - plus library-level parse-only throughput vs Rust parsers (quick-xml, roxmltree) on PubMed 195MB, 1MB attribute-heavy XML, 1MB patent XML, and a 69KB SVG.
claimed_speedup: vs pugixml: 2.6x on DBLP 5.1GB //article (3.2s vs 8.3s), 1.3x on PubMed 195MB //MeshHeading, 1.7x on 10MB attribute-heavy //record, 2.6x on the Ryzen 9 attribute-heavy case; vs xmllint: up to 17.5x; vs quick-xml (Rust): 1.1-4.0x depending on file shape
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release with [profile.release] lto=true, codegen-units=1, strip=true; CLI benchmarks use hyperfine (5 warmup, 20 runs), library benchmarks use criterion
hardware: Apple M4 Max (NEON) and AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (AVX2)
tradeoffs: Produces a flat structural-index array (no DOM tree, ~16 bytes/tag vs ~35 for a DOM node) rather than pugixml's tree API; pugixml still wins on scalar-aggregation (count()) and text-predicate (contains()) queries where its single-pass DOM build has lower overhead; it's a Rust crate, so C++ consumers need an FFI layer; no top-level LICENSE file is committed - the MIT OR Apache-2.0 grant lives only in Cargo.toml package metadata.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (project's own README and bench/ scripts), not independently reproduced, but methodology is unusually complete for a solo project: exact CPU models, hyperfine warmup/run counts, pinned release-profile flags, and public corpus-download scripts are all in the repo.
found_via: WebSearch '"XML parsing" SIMD paper 2024 2025 faster arXiv' surfaced a github.com/cigrainger/simdxml search hit, which resolved to the canonical github.com/simdxml/simdxml repo

name: teptris
workload: Min-of-10 in-memory parse throughput (MB/s) on a seeded 9-file synthetic TOML corpus (array_heavy, cargo_like, datetime_heavy, deep_tables, mixed, scalar_float, scalar_int, scalar_string, table_heavy; 248KB-1.5MB each) against tomlplusplus v3.4.0, tomlc99, tomlc17, cpptoml, and toml11 v4.2.0.
claimed_speedup: 3.2-7.5x faster than tomlplusplus v3.4.0 across all 9 shapes in the run-3 table (e.g. array_heavy 312 vs 60 MB/s, table_heavy 256 vs 38 MB/s); later profiling rounds report teptris as 5.2-8.2x the best competitor per shape (toml++ is the best C++ competitor on most rows); also 2.0-2.8x tomlc17, 1.9-3.5x cpptoml where they parse, and 100-1000x toml11 (the project attributes toml11's slowness to its per-token error-location metadata, not a fair fast-path comparison)
tradeoffs: Pure C99, zero-copy parsing (input buffer must stay alive for the document's lifetime), passes toml-test 714/714 (TOML 1.1 view) and 711/711 (1.0 view); Ruby/Python bindings were initially far slower than the C core due to per-node FFI crossings, since partly closed by native-binding + bulk-drain work but bindings still trail the core's raw speedup.
caveats: Numbers are first-party (the project's own benchmark ledger), but hardware, compiler, and flags are all explicitly pinned, and the corpus generator plus competing-library commit pins are published in-repo, meeting the Tier-A bar on methodology transparency. Very new (repo created 2026-09-13), 0 stars, from the same small org behind sibling projects leptris/yeptris - unaudited beyond its own CI. The 100-1000x toml11 figure looks implausible at face value; the project itself flags toml11 as running a differently-scoped (error-location-tracking) code path, so treat that specific ratio with caution.
found_via: GitHub search 'fast toml' --sort stars, which surfaced leptris/teptris directly; benchmarks/LEDGER.md opened for methodology

name: libleptris
workload: SAX/DOM parse, attribute lookup, text extraction, and 10 XPath queries on ~1-5KB XML fixtures vs libxml2; separately, DOM write/serialize (attribute set, 10k-child append, 2MB serialize) vs pugixml.
claimed_speedup: vs libxml2: SAX 2.5-3.6x, DOM parse 1.4x, attribute lookup 1.9x, text extraction 2.6x, indexed child access 1.09x, XPath 1.3-4.0x (wins all 10 XPath benchmarks); vs pugixml: attribute-set ~25x and serialize attr-heavy 1.6x faster, but 1.3x slower on bulk child-append and 1.1x slower on text-heavy serialize
compiler_and_flags: clang -O3 -flto=thin (LTO is the default for Release/RelWithDebInfo builds)
hardware: "Apple Silicon" (exact CPU model not stated; benchmarked on GitHub Actions macos-latest runners)
tradeoffs: C99 API with FFI-based Ruby and cffi-based Python bindings; pool-based memory model (single leptris_document_free call); keeps whitespace-only text nodes by default to match libxml2 fidelity (costs ~1.1-1.4x vs pugixml's default unless LEPTRIS_PARSE_DROP_WS_TEXT is set); no XML Schema 1.1 or XQuery support; loses to pugixml on bulk child-append and text-heavy serialize.
caveats: Hardware is reported only as generic 'Apple Silicon' via a GitHub Actions macos-latest runner, not a pinned CPU model, so this falls short of full Tier-A reproducibility even though benchmark code and CI are public. Part of a 3-repo family (leptris/yeptris/teptris) from the same very young GitHub org (this repo created Nov 2025, 1 star) - an emerging, largely unaudited project.
found_via: GitHub search 'fast xml parser' --language=C++ --sort stars surfaced patrickbr/pfxml and mls-m5/fast-xml (both rejected as no-benchmark); a follow-up search 'fast toml' --sort stars surfaced leptris/teptris, whose README named sibling repo leptris/leptris (libleptris)

name: RapidXml
workload: DOM parse of synthetic wide/shallow and deep/narrow XML files at sizes from 1KB to 100MB, each library in its own Docker container on a GitHub Actions runner, measuring wall time/throughput/memory/CPU (bemayer/xml-benchmark cross-language shootout, 14 libraries across 7 languages)
claimed_speedup: RapidXml throughput of 1084.9 MB/s vs libxml2's 278.8 MB/s (~3.9x) at 10MB; 638.2 vs 161.2 MB/s (~4.0x) at 100MB; 2017.2 vs 3277.1 MB/s at 100KB where libxml2 is actually faster at that size (derived from page data) -- RapidXml consistently beats libxml2 at 10MB+ but not always at small sizes, and does not beat pugixml at any size in this suite
compiler_and_flags: g++ via CMake Release build (per benchmarks/rapidxml/CMakeLists.txt: `cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`); exact flags/version not published in the report
hardware: ubuntu-latest GitHub Actions runner (exact CPU model not published)
stars_or_usage: 2 stars on this GitHub host of the code; the library itself is widely embedded/vendored (used as the RapidXml reference implementation in multiple independent XML-parser shootouts, e.g. bemayer/xml-benchmark and the SpeedyXml-cpp benchmark)
tradeoffs: In-situ, destructive parser (mutates the source buffer); allocates DOM nodes from an internal per-instance pool, which becomes a scaling bottleneck at large file sizes versus newer arena/SoA designs (see libsimdxml and parshred entries, both of which cite this exact weakness); C++03-era single-header code with no active upstream maintainer since the 1.13 release (2009); canonical home is SourceForge (http://rapidxml.sourceforge.net/), this GitHub repo is a maintained third-party host of the original source
caveats: Independent third-party benchmark suite (not RapidXml's own repo) shows it beating libxml2 by ~4x at 10MB/100MB, but the suite also shows RapidXml losing to pugixml at every size tested -- only libxml2 should be cited as the beaten baseline here, not pugixml; hardware is a generic CI runner (no CPU model stated), which caps the tier at B rather than A; the original project has had no upstream release since 2009, only community forks/mirrors remain active

name: libsimdxml
workload: Parsing synthetic XML files (1-30MB, deep nesting up to 22 levels, attributes, entities, CDATA, comments, PIs) into a SIMD-built structural index, single-threaded, measuring MB/s and peak RSS against pugixml 1.16 (in-situ) and libxml2 DOM
claimed_speedup: 1.19x/1.15x/1.24x faster than pugixml 1.16 at 1/5/10 MB (e.g. 245.7 vs 206.3 MB/s at 1MB); roughly 8-10x faster than libxml2 DOM (245.7 vs 28.5 MB/s at 1MB; 296.5 vs 38.0 MB/s at 10MB, derived from page data); also beats Rust's quick-xml by 1.26x-1.47x in the same cross-language run

name: SpeedyXml (SpeedyXml-cpp)
workload: Single-core, streaming SAX-style push parse of a 235 MiB real-world XML document, comparing wall-clock time against pugixml (DOM), RapidXml (in-situ DOM), libxml2 (SAX2 streaming), and Expat (streaming); repeated across 8 additional public XML datasets via a bundled script
claimed_speedup: 0.34s vs libxml2's 1.53s on the 235MiB document (~4.4x faster, both streaming parsers); also faster than the DOM parsers pugixml (2.9x) and RapidXml (3.7x), though the author notes those two are not directly comparable since they hold the whole document in memory; ~680 MiB/s overall; author states 'no other parser reaches half of SpeedyXml's throughput' across the public dataset set
tradeoffs: Streaming SAX-like push model only, not a DOM (caller must build any tree themselves); does not support XML entity declarations with internal DTD subsets, no namespace resolution, UTF-8-only, requires a little-endian machine
caveats: No CPU model or compiler/flags are disclosed in the README, despite the benchmark being reproducible from source (`cmake -DBUILD_BENCHMARK=ON`, `./bench <file>`, plus tools/public_bench.sh for public datasets); the pugixml/RapidXml comparisons are DOM-vs-streaming and explicitly flagged by the author as not fully apples-to-apples, so the libxml2 comparison (both streaming) is the fairer evidence cited here; very new, low-star project with no third-party corroboration
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "faster than libxml2" (tcShadowWalker/SpeedyXml-cpp)
